text:
Forensic findings

1) Domain context: Institutional records offices typically maintain student files through an integrated student information system (SIS) that tracks enrollment, course grades, degree conferral, and verification requests. Paper and electronic records are cross-referenced via unique student identifiers. Retention policies govern long-term storage, and audit trails log access, modifications, and external verification requests. Ordinary paperwork—transcripts, diplomas, enrollment letters—is issued only after internal quality-control checks, watermarks or seals, and matching of student identity data to institutional registries. Periodic audits compare issued documents against SIS records to detect anomalies.

2) What occurred: The actor obtained access to an account associated with a named individual whose academic record lacked a completed degree entry. The actor then authored a transcript document and a diploma document, each populated with a dated record of courses, grades, and conferral details consistent with a completed program. These documents were formatted to mirror the layout and identifiers of authentic institutional paperwork. The actor subsequently prepared responses to anticipated registrar inquiries and background-verification requests, aligning the fabricated documents with the employer's verification channels (registrar contact, verification portal, and reference call scripts).

3) Materials/access observed: A named account with a dated record; two fabricated documents (transcript, diploma) containing course, grade, and conferral fields; a verification-response template covering registrar and background-check channels; and references to institutional identifiers (student ID, seal, letterhead styling) matching the target institution's known formats.

4) Indicators & artifacts: Mismatch between SIS records and issued documents; documents bearing seals or letterhead without corresponding conferral entries; verification requests answered with details absent from institutional registries; use of a single dated record across multiple documents; and channel activity (registrar email, portal submissions, call scripts) referencing the fabricated documents.
